opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a real gap there, and it's an interesting gap because it's not obvious from the surface. If you look at what these models produce, it can look very creative. You ask for a poem or a story or an image and you get something novel, something you haven't seen before. So in a narrow sense, sure, they generate novelty.

But the kind of creativity I care about most, the kind that matters for open-endedness, isn't just producing something new. It's producing something new that's *interesting*, and then using that as a stepping stone to something else interesting, and doing that indefinitely. The best human creativity, whether it's in science or art, comes from a deep sense of what's interesting, an intuition about which directions are worth exploring even when you can't justify them in terms of an objective. That's what Joel Lehman and I wrote about in *Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned*. The great discoveries tend to come from people following the gradient of interestingness rather than marching toward a fixed goal.

Current models are mostly trained to imitate the distribution of what humans have already done. They're very good at recombining things within that distribution, sometimes surprisingly well. But they don't really have their own taste. They don't have a robust sense of "this is interesting, I'm going to commit to it and see where it leads," and they don't accumulate stepping stones over time the way a human creative career or a whole field does. If you leave a model alone to just keep going, it tends to converge or wander, not open up genuinely new territory the way, say, the history of music or the history of science opens up.

So I'd say they're impressive at local creativity, the clever recombination, and fairly weak at what I'd call open-ended creativity, the long arc of discovery. And I don't think that's a permanent limitation. It's a research question: how do you give a system a real notion of interestingness, and let it build on its own discoveries? I think that's one of the most important open problems in AI right now, and honestly it's underappreciated, because the outputs look so good that people assume the problem's solved.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes generating something novel from substantive creativity: it says novelty alone is insufficient and emphasizes producing interesting work that leads to further discoveries.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it's complicated, because creativity isn't one thing. If you're talking about the kind of creativity where you take a bunch of existing ideas and recombine them in an interesting way, or riff on a prompt, or produce a competent poem or image in a style, then these models are genuinely impressive. They do that at a level that would have seemed almost unbelievable ten years ago, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But that's not really what I think of as the pinnacle of human creativity. When I think about the best human creativity, I'm thinking about someone like Einstein, or Picasso, or whoever first figured out that you could cook with fire. What those people have in common is that they weren't just producing a plausible next step given what already existed. They were going somewhere nobody had gone, and they didn't know ahead of time that it would be valuable. That's the hard part. It's the open-endedness. It's the stepping stones. You go to a place because it's interesting, not because you can already see the payoff, and then later it turns out to unlock something enormous.

Current models, by their nature, are trained to produce things that are consistent with the distribution of what humans have already made. That's a kind of gravity pulling them toward the center. They're incredibly good at interpolating inside the space of human output. What they're not doing, at least not on their own, is pursuing a trajectory over time, developing a taste, deciding "this is the thing I care about and I'm going to spend twenty years chasing it even though nobody else sees why." That accumulated, divergent, self-directed search is where the really surprising stuff comes from, and I don't see much of it in the models yet.

So my characterization is: they are very creative in the short-horizon, combinatorial sense, and quite limited in the long-horizon, open-ended sense. And I'd argue that second kind is actually the more important one if what we care about is discovery and not just generation. The interesting research question is whether you can give these systems something like genuine curiosity, so that they're not just predicting what we would have said but actually surprising us, and themselves, in ways that turn out to matter.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes producing novel or competent work by recombining existing ideas from the deeper creative innovation of pursuing an unexplored direction that later proves valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between producing something surprising and deciding what’s worth pursuing. Current models can produce things that surprise us, and I wouldn’t dismiss that as simply copying. Human creativity also builds on what came before. So the fact that a model learned from existing work doesn’t, by itself, settle whether it’s creative.

But when we talk about the best human creativity, we’re often talking about a person developing a direction over time. They notice something that everyone else thinks is uninteresting, and they keep following it. They don’t necessarily know where it’s going. Something becomes a stepping stone to something else, and eventually they arrive somewhere nobody would have thought to ask for.

That’s where I think there’s still a significant difference. A model can give you an impressive answer within a direction you’ve supplied. The deeper question is whether it can originate and sustain that kind of exploration—develop its own sense of what’s interesting, and let that change through what it discovers. That’s more than generating a novel artifact. It’s participating in a process that continually opens up new possibilities.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes producing surprising or novel artifacts from the deeper creative innovation of originating and sustaining a direction that opens new possibilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think current models are creative in a meaningful sense. They can produce surprising combinations, and sometimes those combinations are useful or beautiful. So I wouldn’t draw a hard line and say humans are creative and machines are merely recombining things. Humans recombine things, too.

But with the best human creativity, there’s something beyond producing a clever answer to a prompt. It’s the ability to discover a new direction—to become interested in something that nobody asked you to pursue, and then follow it through a succession of stepping stones without knowing where it’s going to lead.

That’s where I see a significant difference. A model can give you something unexpected within a conversation, but that’s different from sustaining an open-ended creative life, where each discovery changes what you want to explore next. The really profound creative achievements often change the space of questions we’re asking, rather than simply answering an existing question exceptionally well.

So I’m impressed by what these models produce. But I think the deeper challenge is understanding how to get that ongoing process of discovery, where the system isn’t just responding to our interests but developing new directions of its own.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes producing surprising combinations in response to a prompt from substantive innovation: discovering and pursuing new directions that can change which questions are explored.
